chapter: Classical roots and the future of jazz
title: Classical composers, orphanage music and the staying power of jazz
summary: Armstrong lists the classical composers he played in the orphanage and brass bands, discusses foreign arrangers and symphonic hot-man work, and dismisses fads like bop and rock and roll.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I mean, Faby has only very little time left. Mr. Armstrong, this is interesting. Of the American composers today, saying the symphonic theme or an opera, who do you like best?

Even when I was in school, I played all classical music. When I was in the orphanage, we played duets. And that was the music. So that instills the soul in you. You know? Litz, Bach, Bach, Marnonoff, Gustav Mahler, and Haydn. We had a little laugh there, where he kept on saying, Haydn, Haydn. And I said, well, let him come out. You know? That was Haydn's style, too. He'd surprise you any time. Every composer that there was, we used it in this song. I'm glad you mentioned Mahler. He's one of my favorite composers. Yeah. And that's it. That's it, when he said, Gustav Mahler, I said, well, don't forget, Spatz Mahler. Well, he was a composer, too, but later music, you know? I think, chronologically, if those greats, the great symphonic composers, had been around today, I think they would have adapted themselves to our music and been just as great. I mean, Well, that's what the musicians showed appreciation by playing their music in swing time. That's why I say the foreign arrangers did so much for America because they brought all that, because that's all they played. And look what the Three Penny Opera did for Mac the Knife. You understand? Yes, of course. Probably they all played classical music for years, and that's where they read, them musicians, read and everything. I mean, no insinuation or anything like that, but you wonder, are they good musicians? Well, they're good musicians in front. See? Now, they come to America and they say, well, look at you. That's the one that's the little beat in it. Yes. Probably wouldn't bear it in their mind. And they're the one that brought the idea to us, which I'm very grateful and I meet them all over the world. See? So we all have something in common to thank each other, appreciate each other, every musician you meet. There's a lot of English bands. That boy came over here and his ovation was so big at the Carnegie Hall, they had to put the lights out. He had took a hundred boughs. So he had to put the lights out and he's from England. Tramon player. He played all kind of classics. And I think you got to be a good musician in the heart. You know. You got to have that equipment there to call on it. classical background of someone. See? And them brass bands was a lot of experience for me. Then comes into this symphony orchestra and I'm playing at a nightclub and they only hired me to be the hot man in the band. Because when the lights goes up, they play an overture. You know. And there was days where when they play a tune like Spanish Shaw or something like that, well that's where I come in. But still in all, I got to work when the lights go out. So when you look around, I'm sitting there playing second trumpet one week. And first trumpet one week. And your environment makes you. You got to improve if you enjoy or want to get someplace in there and you enjoy what you're doing. How can I miss? All they have to worry about the different divisions and the classical music. You know how those different. Well I'm sitting there getting a million dollar experience and they getting the experience from the beat. that ain't still in there. Fifteen pieces. What do you think all these things that are happening like rock and roll and bop and way out and that stuff, where are we going to be? Are we going to be around forever? Just keep blowing your horn, perhaps. Because probably just like anything else they'll fall for a fad. Fads just last so long. You haven't heard the word bop until I just mentioned it. That's for years. Yeah. It's just like I remember one time I was a kid and there's a fellow at the gate telling, right this way folks see the horse's head where his tail ought to be. See, everybody is climbing to pay this dime and get in there the guy that's got a horse turned around. Well that one time he got away with it. That's the same as all that jujitsu music. You know but they can't make a rebound and they can't return trip like we were. We go to the same place four or five times a year and you have the same audience. Same as Heifetz, Marion Anderson. You don't need 9,000 weeks advertising. You don't have to build up because the people who get the tickets they ain't saying a word. But we look around and there's the audience right there. We played Carnegie Hall night after Christmas. See? All the stars will be jizz. You know what I mean? So it's just another date when I walk out on that stage. I play the same thing that I played down in the arena in the same way. I'd stand on your head even. Then we all agree that it's here to stay. Cut and stay. Keep it swinging. Don't worry about it. Bob Hacken's doing all right. Sure is. Jack's doing all right but he's bad. I'm sure that Bunny and Bix are doing all right too.
